title: What are the three pillars of observability (metrics, logs, traces), and how do they complement each other in a distributed system?
shortTitle: The three pillars of observability (metrics, logs, traces) and how they complement each other
topicTitle: What are the three pillars of observability

s1_definition.profdef: The three pillars of observability are metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics are numeric time-series that answer "how much and how fast" cheaply and continuously, such as request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles. Logs are timestamped, discrete records of individual events that answer "what exactly happened" with full context. Traces follow a single request as it travels across multiple services, answering "where did the time go and which hop failed." Together they let you detect a problem (metrics), locate the failing hop (traces), and understand the root cause (logs).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India processing a transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001. Metrics are the dashboard in the manager's office showing "500 transfers per minute, 2 failing" — a quick pulse, but no detail about any single transfer. Logs are the detailed diary each department keeps: "10:05:03 validated Rajesh's balance, 10:05:04 debited 50000." Traces are the stamped journey slip that travels WITH the transfer form through every department, recording the time spent at each counter, so you can see the fraud-check counter took four seconds while all others took milliseconds. The dashboard tells you something is wrong, the journey slip tells you which counter is slow, and the diary tells you exactly why.
s1_definition.oneliner: Metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The three pillars of observability are metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics are numeric time-series that answer "how much and how fast" cheaply and continuously, such as request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles. Logs are timestamped, discrete records of individual events that answer "what exactly happened" with full context. Traces follow a single request as it travels across multiple services, answering "where did the time go and which hop failed." Together they let you detect a problem (metrics), locate the failing hop (traces), and understand the root cause (logs).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India processing a transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001. Metrics are the dashboard in the manager's office showing "500 transfers per minute, 2 failing" — a quick pulse, but no detail about any single transfer. Logs are the detailed diary each department keeps: "10:05:03 validated Rajesh's balance, 10:05:04 debited 50000." Traces are the stamped journey slip that travels WITH the transfer form through every department, recording the time spent at each counter, so you can see the fraud-check counter took four seconds while all others took milliseconds. The dashboard tells you something is wrong, the journey slip tells you which counter is slow, and the diary tells you exactly why.

**One line to remember:** Metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why.

sections.s2_technical:
Metrics are aggregated numbers measured over time. A metric like `http_requests_total` or `transfer_latency_seconds` is cheap to store because it is just numbers bucketed by time and a few labels, so you can keep them for a long time and query them fast. Metrics power dashboards and alerts — "error rate above one percent for five minutes, page the on-call engineer." Their weakness is that they are aggregated: a metric tells you two percent of transfers failed, but not which transfers or why. You deliberately keep metric labels low-cardinality (service, status, endpoint) and you never put a customer id or a transfer id in a label, because that would explode storage.

Logs are individual event records, usually structured as JSON with a timestamp, a level, a message, and context fields. A log line can carry the full detail — the account ids, the amount, the exception stack trace — that a metric cannot. Logs answer "what exactly happened to THIS request." Their weakness is volume and cost: logging every event for millions of requests is expensive, and searching raw logs across many services is slow unless they are centralized in a system like Elasticsearch or Loki. This is why high-cardinality identifiers belong in logs, not metric labels.

Traces solve the distributed-system problem. In a microservices bank, one transfer might touch the API gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, the account service, and the notification service. A trace assigns one trace id to the whole request and a span id to each hop, and propagates the trace id through every call. The result is a waterfall view showing exactly how long each service took and where an error occurred. Traces answer "across all these services, where did my request spend its time and which hop failed." Their weakness is that tracing every request is expensive, so teams often sample — keeping all error traces but only a fraction of successful ones.

The pillars complement each other through correlation. The standard workflow is: a metric alert fires (error rate spiked). You open the trace for a failing request and see the fraud service span is red. You pivot from that trace to the logs for that exact trace id — because you propagated the trace id into every log line — and read the exception that explains why. OpenTelemetry is the industry standard that unifies all three: it emits metrics, logs, and traces with a shared trace id and resource attributes, so you can jump between them seamlessly. A senior nuance: observability is not just "having the three pillars" but being able to ask new questions you did not anticipate — which requires high-cardinality context in logs and traces, and exemplars that link a metric spike directly to a sample trace.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service is reporting that some transfers are slow. The on-call engineer needs to find out why using the three pillars.

Problem 1 — The engineer first needs a cheap, always-on signal that something is wrong. This is the metrics pillar: a running count of transfers, a count of failures, and latency measurements. When failures cross a threshold, an alert fires.

Problem 2 — Once alerted, the engineer needs to know WHERE the slowness is. This is the traces pillar: a single transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 is traced across validation, fraud-check, debit, credit, and notification spans, revealing that fraud-check is the slow hop.

Problem 3 — Knowing fraud-check is slow, the engineer needs to know WHY. This is the logs pillar: the detailed log lines for that trace id show the fraud service retried a downstream call three times.

Our runnable Java simulation models all three pillars for a transfer: a `MetricsRegistry` with counters and a latency recorder, a `Tracer` that creates a trace with named spans and durations, and structured logging via java.util.logging. The `TransferService` emits all three while processing a transfer, and the demo prints the dashboard snapshot, the trace waterfall, and the correlated logs. Classes: `MetricsRegistry`, `Span`, `Tracer`, `TransferService`, and an `ObservabilityDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — structured JSON logging with trace id

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml — structured logs carry the traceId for correlation -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
      <!-- traceId from MDC lets logs be correlated with traces -->
      <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>
      <includeMdcKeyName>spanId</includeMdcKeyName>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="JSON"/>
  </root>
</configuration>
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a single transfer of 50000 rupees from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001, where the fraud-check hop is unusually slow.

Step 1: The service starts the transfer and creates a trace with a unique trace id. Every log line it writes from now on includes that trace id, which is what makes later correlation possible.

Step 2: The validate span runs in three milliseconds and a log line records the validation. The metric counters have not yet changed because the transfer is still in progress.

Step 3: The fraud-check span runs and takes 4200 milliseconds because it retried a downstream call three times. A warning log line records the retries, and the span is added to the trace as the dominant chunk of time.

Step 4: The debit, credit, and notify spans each run in a few milliseconds and are logged at fine level with the same trace id.

Step 5: The transfer completes. The metrics registry records one successful transfer with a latency over four seconds, which pushes up the p95 latency metric. The dashboard snapshot now shows the elevated p95.

Step 6: The engineer reads the metrics snapshot and sees high p95. They open the trace waterfall and see fraud-check is the slow hop. They pivot to the logs filtered by that trace id and read the retry warning, which is the root cause. All three pillars together completed the diagnosis.

```
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — observability demo for a slow transfer
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] [trace=a3f91c20] validating transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [WARNING] [trace=a3f91c20] fraud-check slow: retried downstream 3x
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] [trace=a3f91c20] transfer COMPLETED in 4225ms
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] METRICS snapshot: transfers_total=1 failed=0 error_rate=0.00% p95_latency=4225ms
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] TRACE waterfall:
trace a3f91c20:
    validate            3ms ok
    fraud-check      4200ms ok
    debit               5ms ok
    credit              5ms ok
    notify             12ms ok
2026-10-30 01:50:44 [INFO   ] Diagnosis: metrics showed high p95, trace pinpointed fraud-check, logs explained the 3 downstream retries.
```

```
  [HEALTHY] ──metric alert──→ [INVESTIGATING] ──open trace──→ [LOCATED hop]
                                                                   │
                                                        pivot to logs by traceId
                                                                   ▼
                                                             [ROOT CAUSE FOUND]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. service.transfer(SAV2001, CUR3001, 50000, tracer)
  2.   → log.info("[trace=..] validating")      (LOGS)
  3.   → tracer.addSpan("validate", 3, false)    (TRACES)

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The three pillars of observability are metrics, logs, and traces, and the way I summarise them is that metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where it is wrong, and logs tell you why. Metrics are cheap numeric time-series like request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles; they run continuously, power dashboards and alerts, and are the always-on pulse of the system. Their limitation is that they are aggregated, so I keep their labels low-cardinality and never put a customer id or transfer id in a metric label.

Logs are discrete, timestamped event records, ideally structured as JSON, that carry the full detail a metric cannot — the account ids, the amount, the exception stack trace. They answer what exactly happened to a specific request. Their limitation is volume and cost, which is why high-cardinality identifiers live in logs rather than metric labels, and why logs are centralized in a system like Elasticsearch or Loki so they can be searched across many services. Traces solve the distributed-system problem: one trace id is attached to a request and propagated through every service it touches, and each hop becomes a span, producing a waterfall that shows exactly where the time went and which hop failed.

The real power is not in having the three pillars separately but in correlating them. In my project at the National Bank of India, when transfers between Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 went slow, a metric alert fired on high p99 latency. I opened a trace for a slow transfer and the waterfall showed the fraud-check span taking over four seconds while every other span took milliseconds. Because we propagated the trace id into every log line, I pivoted from that trace directly to the logs filtered by the trace id and read that the fraud service had retried a downstream call three times — the root cause. We standardise on OpenTelemetry so all three pillars share one trace id and we can jump between a Grafana metric, a Jaeger trace, and the Loki logs seamlessly. The principle I always state is that observability is the ability to answer questions you did not anticipate, and that requires all three pillars stitched together by a common trace id.
